note.specFocus: Christian teaching on sin, the Fall, and how Christians try to overcome selfishness, greed, ignorance and wrongdoing.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.3 Selfishness, Greed, Ignorance and Sin
Sin is central to Christian teaching about the human condition: it describes anything that falls short of God's standards and damages a person's relationship with God and with others.
The Fall and Original Sin
• Genesis 3 tells of Adam and Eve disobeying God's one command by eating fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, despite the serpent's temptation. This act, the Fall, is traditionally understood to have introduced sin and death into the world.
• Original Sin is the belief that every human inherits this tendency towards selfishness and wrongdoing; Romans 3:23 summarises this starkly: "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God".
Forms of wrongdoing
• Selfishness and greed: putting one's own wants above the needs of others or of God, condemned throughout the Bible, for example in the Ten Commandments' prohibition on coveting (Exodus 20:17).
• Ignorance: failing to know or follow God's will, sometimes through a hardened conscience rather than a simple lack of information.
• Sin as "missing the mark": the biblical concept of sin (Greek hamartia) pictures wrongdoing as falling short of a target — God's standard of holiness and love — rather than only breaking specific rules.
Overcoming sin
• Christians believe forgiveness and reconciliation with God are possible through confession, repentance (turning away from sin) and faith in Jesus' death and resurrection, which Christians believe atones for sin.
• Regular practices such as confession (especially in the Catholic Church), prayer and following Jesus' teaching and example are seen as ways of resisting selfishness and growing in goodness.
Exam link: for "Identify" questions, give specific concrete examples (e.g. theft, pride, dishonesty); for "Explain" questions, connect sin back to the Fall and to the need for forgiveness through Christ.

questions.examTip: Give three distinct, relevant facts. One clear point earns each mark; development is not required for this question type.
questions.modelAnswer:
A clear three-point response could be:

1. Breaking one of the Ten Commandments, such as stealing, murder or adultery (Exodus 20).
2. Failing to love God and love one's neighbour, which Jesus taught were the two greatest commandments (Mark 12:30–31).
3. Pride or self-centredness that puts one's own will above God's will, which many Christians see as the root of sin shown in Adam and Eve's disobedience in Genesis 3.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Most Christians trace the origin of sin to the Fall in Genesis 3, where Adam and Eve disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit; this is traditionally called Original Sin and is understood to have affected all of humanity, leaving people naturally inclined towards wrongdoing.

Second, Sin is often defined as "missing the mark" or falling short of what God intends; Romans 3:23 states that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God", meaning sin is seen as a universal human condition rather than something only a few people do.

Finally, Christians believe sin damages a person's relationship with God, but that through Jesus' death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God become possible; this is why confession, repentance and grace are central to Christian teaching about overcoming sin.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of moral choices, temptation, original sin, repentance and grace and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
